Case Name:

Nese v. Cavafian, et al.

SPECIAL MOTION TO STRIKE
[CCP § 425.16]
Moving Party:

Defendant, Gary Cavafian
Responding Party:

Plaintiff, John F. Nese
RELIEF REQUESTED:

Strike the Complaint and award attorneys’ fees and costs in the amount of $62,700.00.

CAUSES OF ACTION: from Complaint
1)
Civil Harassment

Abuse of Process

Invasion of Privacy
REQUEST FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE:

The Court may take judicial notice of “[r]ecords of (1) any court of this state or (2) any court of record of the United States or of any state of the United States.” (Evidence Code § 452, subd. (d).)
The court, however, may not take judicial notice of the truth of the contents of the documents. (Herrera v. Deutsche Bank National Trust Co. (2011) 196 Cal.App.4th 1366, 1375.) Documents are only judicially noticeable to show their existence and what orders were made such that the truth of the facts and findings within the documents are not judicially noticeable. (Lockley v. Law Office of Cantrell, Green, Pekich, Cruz & McCort (2001) 91 Cal.App.4th 875, 885.)
Pursuant to Plaintiff’s request, the Court takes judicial notice of the Notice of Motion and Motion to Continue Hearing and Permit Discovery filed in this action on March 9, 2026 and the Declaration of Mary O. O’Neill filed in support thereof. (RJN, Ex. A.)

SUMMARY OF FACTS:

Plaintiff John F. Nese (“Plaintiff”) owns the real property located at 92 Pinecrest Drive, South Pasadena, California 91301. Defendant Gary Cavafian (“Defendant”) owns the adjacent property, located at 84 Pinecrest Drive, South Pasadena, California 91301. According to the Complaint, in the Spring of 2023 Plaintiff began demolishing the existing structure on his property and preparing the site for new construction. Plaintiff alleges that, since that time, Defendant has continuously attempted to interfere with the construction.
The Complaint alleges that Defendant has repeatedly moved surveyor stakes marking the property boundaries. The Complaint alleges that Defendant installed cameras aimed directly at Plaintiff’s property to surveil the project and the people coming onto the site. The Complaint alleges that Defendant has submitted numerous complaints to various agencies—including the City of South Pasadena, Cal OSHA, the AQMD, the Department of Sanitation, and the County of Los Angeles Fire Department—asserting construction-related violations. According to the Complaint, no violations have been identified by any agency, and the complaints are unfounded.
ANALYSIS:

Code of Civil Procedure section 425.16 permits the Court to strike causes of action arising from an act in furtherance of the defendant's right of free speech or petition, unless the plaintiff establishes that there is a probability that the plaintiff will prevail on the claim.
“The anti-SLAPP procedures are designed to shield a defendant’s constitutionally protected conduct from the undue burden of frivolous litigation.” (Baral v. Schnitt (2016) 1 Cal.5th 376, 393.) “The anti-SLAPP statute does not insulate defendants from any liability for claims arising from the protected rights of petition or speech. It only provides a procedure for weeding out, at an early stage, meritless claims arising from protected activity.” (Id. at 384.)
“Resolution of an anti-SLAPP motion involves two steps. First, the defendant must establish that the challenged claim arises from activity protected by section 425.16. If the defendant makes the required showing, the burden shifts to the plaintiff to demonstrate the merit of the claim by establishing a probability of success.” (Baral, supra, 1 Cal.5th at 384, citation omitted.) The California Supreme Court has “described this second step as a ‘summary-judgment-like procedure.’ The court does not weigh evidence or resolve conflicting factual claims. Its inquiry is limited to whether the plaintiff has stated a legally sufficient claim and made a prima facie factual showing sufficient to sustain a favorable judgment. It accepts the plaintiff’s evidence as true, and evaluates the defendant’s showing only to determine if it defeats the plaintiff’s claim as a matter of law. ‘[C]laims with the requisite minimal merit may proceed.’” (Id. at 384-385 [citations omitted].) The anti-SLAPP motion need not address what the complaint alleges is an entire cause of action and may seek to strike only those portions which describe protected activity. (Id. at 395-396.)
Defendant moves to strike the Complaint on grounds that Plaintiff’s claims against him arise from protected petitioning activity in connection with issues under consideration, or reviewable, by various governmental bodies, including municipal code enforcement, Cal/OSHA, AQMD, and fire and sanitation authorities.
Protected Activity
To satisfy the first prong of the two-prong test, a movant defendant must demonstrate that the act or acts of which the plaintiff complains were taken ‘in furtherance of the defendant’s right of petition or free speech under the United States or California Constitution in connection with a public as defined in the statute. (Equilon Enterprises v. Consumer Cause, Inc. (2002) 29 Cal.4th 53, 67; see also City of Cotati v. Cashman (2002) 29 Cal.4th 69, 78 [“[i]n the anti-SLAPP context, the critical point is whether the plaintiff's cause of action itself was based on an act in furtherance of the defendant's right of petition or free speech”].) Section 425.16 expressly “defines the types of claims that are subject to the anti-SLAPP procedures…as these terms are defined in subdivision (e)(1)-(4) of the statute.” (City of Cotati, supra, 29 Cal. 4th at pp. 75-76.)
As relevant here, an “act in furtherance of a person’s right of petition or free speech under the United States or California Constitution in connection with a public issue” includes: (1) any written or oral statement or writing made before a legislative, executive, or judicial proceeding, or any other official proceeding authorized by law, [and] (2) any written or oral statement or writing made in connection with an issue under consideration or review by a legislative, executive, or judicial body, or any other official proceeding authorized by law, […] of (4) any other conduct in furtherance of the exercise of the constitutional right of petition or the constitutional right of free speech in connection with a public issue or an issue of public interest” (CCP § 425.16 subd. (e).)
First and Third Causes of Action, Civil Harassment and Invasion of Privacy
Here, the first and third causes of action in the Complaint for civil harassment and invasion of privacy are based on the following alleged acts of Defendant:
-
Attempts to “physically stop the work when shoring holes were being installed and poured” (Compl., ¶ 7)
-
Moving surveyor stakes (Compl., ¶ 7.)
-
Installing cameras pointed directly at Plaintiff’s property for surveillance purposes (Compl., ¶¶ 9-10)
-
Videotaping and audio-recording the construction and people coming to the site without their consent (Compl., ¶¶ 11-12, 28-29.)
Defendant argues that documenting the construction is “intertwined speech in connection with issues under governmental review.” (Mot., p. 13:1-2.) Defendant does not cite any cases, however, to support this proposition, nor is the Court aware of any. In determining whether a claim is based on protected activity, the Court will “examine the'principal thrust'or'gravamen'of a plaintiff’s cause of action to determine whether the anti-SLAPP statute applies. [Citation.]” (Optional Capital, Inc. v. Akin Gump Strauss, Hauer & Feld LLP'(2017) 18 Cal.App.5th 95, 110, emphasis in original.) “We assess the principal thrust by identifying ‘[t]he allegedly wrongful and injury-producing'conduct'... that provides the foundation for the claim.’ [Citation.]” (Id. at 111, emphasis in original.) In other words, CCP section 425.16 does not apply if Defendant’s constitutionally protected activity is “merely incidental” or “collateral” to the unprotected activity. (Baral v. Schnitt (2016) 1 Cal.5th 376, 395.)
Here, the wrongful and injury-producing conduct underlying the civil harassment and invasion of privacy causes of action consists of Defendant surveilling and recording Plaintiff’s property without Plaintiff’s consent. (Compl., ¶¶ 7, 9-12, 28-29.) Defendant’s personal behavior towards his neighbor is not a protected activity. Moreover, it cannot be said that Plaintiff’s harassment or invasion of privacy claims “arise from” protected activity because these causes of action are not based on any statements or writings made to governmental agencies. (See CCP § 425.16 subd. (e)(1)-(2).) Defendant argues that his “course of conduct is constitutionally protected because it served a legitimate purpose – documenting and lodging grievances with local and state agencies.” (Mot., p. 14:18-19.) This argument is unavailing. The allegations forming the basis for the harassment and invasion of privacy claims do not arise from Defendant’s statements to the government agencies. (See e.g. Park v. Board of Trustees of California State University (2017) 2 Cal.5th 1057, 1060 [a “claim may be struck only if the speech or petitioning activity itself is the wrong complained of, and not just evidence of liability or a step leading to some different act for which liability is asserted.”].) Defendant’s alleged injury-producing conduct is not insulated under the anti-SLAPP statues simply because Defendant may have used information obtained through the unauthorized surveillance to support his complaints.
Accordingly, Defendant has failed to meet his burden of establishing that the civil harassment and invasion of privacy causes of action arise from protected activity. Thus, the burden does not shift to Plaintiff to demonstrate a probability of prevailing.
The motion is DENIED as to the first and third causes of action.

Second Cause of Action, Abuse of Process
The second cause of action for abuse of process is based on the complaints Defendant lodged with government regulatory agencies, including the City of South Pasadena, Cal/OSHA, AQMD, the Department of Sanitation, and the Los Angeles County Fire Department. (Compl., ¶¶ 17-26.) The Complaint alleges that the “complaints, and each of them are unfounded and without any support. Plaintiff is informed and believes and thereon alleges that the complaints were made for the specific purpose of interfering with the construction on Plaintiffs property and damaging it.” (Compl., ¶ 24.)
Defendant argues that “Regulation of construction impacts, safety compliance, environmental air quality, hazardous materials, and sanitation issues are matters of public concern regularly addressed by municipal code enforcement, Cal/OSHA, AQMD, and fire and sanitation authorities.” (Mot., p. 12:22-25.) In the opposition, Plaintiff argues that this action concerns a property dispute between neighbors, which is not a matter of public interest within the ambit of the anti-SLAPP statutes. (Opp., pp. 4:17-6:18.) Defendant argues that “Matters concerning air quality and pollution, asbestos, workplace safety, and waste management are matters of public concern or public interest.” (Reply, p. 4:9-10.)
To fall under CCP section 425.16 subdivision (e)(4), “the conduct must be in connection with an issue of public interest.” (Weinberg v. Feisel (2003) 110 Cal.App.4th 1122, 1132.) “[A] matter of public interest should be something of concern to a substantial number of people,” and “the assertion of a broad and amorphous public interest is not sufficient.” (Ibid.) “To be considered an issue of public interest, the communication must ‘go beyond the parochial particulars of the given parties.’” (Workman v. Colichman (2019), 33 Cal.App.5th 1039, 1048 [citing Commonwealth Energy Corp. v. Investor Data Exchange, Inc. (2003), 110 Cal.App.4th 26 at 34.)
In his declaration, Defendant asserts: “I contacted the city of South Pasadena to express my concern that the demolition and new construction project of Nese would cause damage to my property, specifically to my house, its foundation, and the land on which it is situated. In this regard, I lodged complaints with the city, contending that the project and proposed plans did not conform to or comply with certain restrictions set forth in the city’s municipal code. My complaints were grievances as to why the city should not approve Nese’s plans or issue the permits he sought.” (Cavafian Decl., ¶ 7.)
Defendant asserts that his complaints to “Cal/OSHA involved safety hazards that [he] observed regarding the excavation of land for Nese’s basement.” (Cavafian Decl., ¶ 7.) Defendant’s complaints to AQMD “involved air and dust pollution [he] observed regarding Nese’s demolition / construction project, and [his] concern was whether those airborne particulates contained asbestos.” (Cavafian Decl., ¶ 7.) Defendant further states that his complaints to the “Department of Sanitation involved oil spill runoffs that were flowing in the sewer drains and cementitious waste related to construction materials.” (Cavafian Decl., ¶ 10.)
Defendant asserts that “these are not private concerns because the effects of airborne asbestos, pollution, and wastewater / oil spill off will not be confined to [Defendant’s] property” (Reply., p. 6:21-23.) This contention vastly overstates the dispute in this case. Defendant’s communications to the City and various regulatory agencies all relate to Defendant’s contention that Plaintiff’s construction project negatively affects his adjacent property. “The fact that a broad and amorphous public interest can be connected to a specific dispute is not sufficient to meet the statutory requirements” of the anti-SLAPP statute. (Workman, supra, 33 Cal.App.5th at p. 1048.)
While in the abstract, society has a general interest in issues of workplace safety, air quality and waste management, these interests are not closely connected to the actual grievances Defendant has lodged here. Simply because some of Defendant’s complaints are related to environmental and safety issues does not convert a private property dispute between neighbors into a topic of public interest. (See, e.g. Bikkina v. Mahadevan (2015) 241 Cal.App.4th 70 [finding that there was no public interest in a dispute regarding statements defendant made about plaintiff’s published climate change research merely because there is public interest in the general topic of climate change].) Defendant’s complaints are part of his private campaign to convince the City to “not approve Nese’s plans or issue the permits he sought.” (Cavafian Decl., ¶ 7.) Defendant has failed to demonstrate that his dispute with Plaintiff is anything other than a private dispute between private parties.
Accordingly, Defendant has failed to meet his burden of establishing that the abuse of process cause of action arises from protected activity under CCP section 425.16 subdivision (e)(4).
The Court notes, however, that the public interest component does not apply to clauses (1) or (2) of CCP section 425.16 subdivision (e). (Blue v. Office of Inspector General (2018) 23 Cal.App.5th 138, 152, review denied (Aug. 22, 2018) [“Instead, if a communication falls within either of the ‘official proceeding’ clauses, the anti-SLAPP statute applies without a separate showing that a public issue or an issue of public interest is present.”].)
Here, Defendant submitted various complaints to regulatory agencies concerning alleged violations, which the agencies subsequently took under consideration and review. (Compl., ¶¶ 19-23.) “[C]ommunication to an official administrative agency designed to prompt action by that agency is as much a part of the official proceeding as a communication made after the proceedings had commenced.” (Computer Xpress, Inc. v. Jakson (2001) 93 Cal.App.4th 993, 1009, internal quotations and citations omitted).
Accordingly, Defendant’s conduct falls within the scope of CCP section 425.16 subdivision (e)(2). Thus, the burden shifts to Plaintiff to establish a probability of prevailing on the merits of the claim.
Probability of Prevailing on the Claim
Once a moving party demonstrates that a cause of action arises from protected conduct, the opposing party must demonstrate that the complaint is both legally sufficient and supported by a sufficient prima facie showing of facts to sustain a favorable judgment if the evidence submitted by the plaintiff is credited. (See Navellier v. Sletten (2002) 29 Cal.4th 82, 88-89.)
“Precisely because the statute (1) permits early intervention in lawsuits alleging unmeritorious causes of action that implicate free speech concerns, and (2) limits opportunity to conduct discovery, the plaintiff's burden of establishing a probability of prevailing is not high: We do not weigh credibility, nor do we evaluate the weight of the evidence. Instead, we accept as true all evidence favorable to the plaintiff and assess the defendant's evidence only to determine if it defeats the plaintiff's submission as a matter of law. Only a cause of action that lacks ‘even minimal merit’ constitutes SLAPP.”  (See Overstock.com, Inc. v. Gradient Analytics, Inc. (2007) 151 Cal.App.4th 688, 699.)
Second Cause of Action, Abuse of Process
“[A]buse of process arises when one uses the court’s process for a purpose other than that for which the process was designed.” (Rusheen v. Cohen (2006) 37 Cal.4th 1048, 1056.) The elements of an abuse of process cause of action are: (1) an ulterior motive by the person using the process; and (2) a willful act in the use of the process not proper in the regular conduct of the proceeding. (Id. at 1057.)''
“Abuse of process consists of ‘[t]he use of the machinery of the legal system for an ulterior motive....’ [citation] Because the purpose of the tort is ‘to preserve the integrity of the court,’ it ‘requires misuse of a judicial process....’ [citation] The tort therefore does not extend to misuse of administrative proceedings, even those involving agencies with ‘quasi-judicial’ powers....’”(Computer Xpress, Inc., supra, 93 Cal.App.4th 993, 1014, [internal citations and quotations omitted].)
Plaintiff’s abuse of process claim alleges that Defendant misused the legal process by filing various complaints with state and local agencies. (Compl., ¶¶ 17-26.) There are no allegations of any misuse of the judicial process. Thus, Plaintiff fails to establish a probability of prevailing on his claim for abuse of process.
The motion is GRANTED as to the second cause of action.

Attorneys’ Fees
A prevailing defendant on a special motion to strike “shall” be entitled to recover its attorney’s fees and costs. (CCP § 425.16(c)(1).) Where a defendant brings a successful motion to strike under section 425.16, these fees are considered mandatory. (Ketchum v. Moses (2001) 24 Cal.4th 1122, 1131.) The fee award should ordinarily include compensation for all hours reasonably spent. (Id., at p. 1141.)
Defendant requests attorneys’ fees and costs in the amount of $62,700.00, which is unreasonable. Defendant only minimally prevailed on the motion. “In determining the lodestar amount, a prevailing party generally may not recover for work on causes of action on which the party was unsuccessful.”  (Mann v. Quality Old Time Service, Inc. (2006) 139 Cal.App.4th 328, 342.) The Court denied the motion with respect to two of the three causes of action. Moreover, 64.3 hours to prepare the motion and 12 hours to prepare the reply is grossly overstated. “A fee request that appears unreasonably inflated is a special circumstance permitting the trial court to reduce the award or deny one altogether.’” (Christian Research Institute v. Alnor'(2008) 165 Cal.App.4th 1315, 1321–1322.) Counsel’s conclusory declaration in support of his fee request does not justify a claim of 78.3 attorney hours at $800 per hour.
The Defendant must file a separate motion for attorney’s fees to be heard on the law and motion calendar.

RULING:

Defendant Gary Cavafian’s Special Motion to Strike is DENIED as to the first and third causes of action and GRANTED as to the second cause of action. The second cause of action is hereby STRICKEN. The Court finds that Defendant is the prevailing party on the motion and entitled to recover attorneys’ fees subject to a separate post-judgment hearing motion for attorney’s fees in light of the Court’s ruling on the Defendant’s Anti-SLAPP motion.
